rationale: B wins because it has better editorial discipline: it turns uncertainty into gates instead of letting inference harden into copy. Its angle "Who is responsible for a flight when no one is flying it?" finds the regulatory story A only treated as supporting proof. A is useful, but "A drone with no pilot is a shot at the inspection business built on pilots" starts writing the displacement story before the update earns it. That is how a decent angle becomes a reporter's first skeptical follow-up.
gaps_in_A: "The launch is the first hard evidence" overclaims. The update says Skydio exited consumer drones two years ago and is launching this product; it does not prove this is the first proof point of the pivot.

"scheduled autonomous flights replace exactly the crewed inspection work an entire services layer sells" is too confident. No cost comparison, contractor displacement, staffing change, or contract-transfer fact was supplied.

"who loses the contract when the dock wins it" is a good reporter question, but A writes it like the answer is already known. It needs to be framed as a question or held until Skydio has deployment proof.

A buries the regulatory issue inside proof language: "what the FAA has authorized" and "FAA authorization status" should probably be its own angle or gating risk, not just homework attached to two other stories.
gaps_in_B: "Story type: customer-story" leads with an angle the set admits is not currently pitchable: "Without a named utility this angle cannot be pitched." True, but then it should be marked conditional, not presented as a live angle.
"The trade desk will take a week-long operations piece if a utility can speak to it" is a little too neat. The utility source is not a garnish; it is the story.
"regulators have been slow to accommodate" may be true, but it is not in the supplied update. That needs a source or softer framing.

"closer to plant equipment than to an aircraft" is smart, but it hangs on buying and budgeting proof the update does not provide. Without pricing or procurement detail, it risks becoming a clever metaphor instead of a story.
